title: What Is a Surrogate Model
lede: A surrogate is a cheap approximation of an expensive simulation or experiment, trained on samples so it predicts outputs in milliseconds.
body: A high-fidelity simulation such as a plasma transport code or a finite-element stress solver can take hours or days per run. Many engineering tasks - optimization, sensitivity studies, uncertainty propagation, real-time control - require thousands or millions of evaluations. A surrogate model (also called a metamodel, emulator, or response surface) replaces the expensive model with a fast statistical or algebraic approximation trained on a limited set of evaluations.

Formally, if the true model is a function y = f(x) mapping inputs x to outputs y, the surrogate f_hat(x) is built from a training set of pairs (x_i, y_i) so that f_hat approximates f well over the input domain while costing orders of magnitude less to evaluate.

Most physical response functions are smooth: nearby inputs produce nearby outputs. Smoothness means a modest number of well-placed samples can pin down the response across the whole domain. The surrogate interpolates or regresses between samples, exploiting continuity that brute-force sampling ignores.
Polynomial response surfaces and polynomial chaos expansions
Gaussian-process regression (kriging), which also returns error bars
Radial basis function and spline interpolants
Reduced-order models built from projection (POD, DMD)
Neural-network and neural-operator surrogates for high-dimensional or field outputs
Choose a design of experiments to place training samples
Run the expensive model at those points
Fit the surrogate and tune its hyperparameters
Deploy for optimization, UQ, or a real-time twin

A surrogate is only trustworthy inside the region it was trained on; extrapolation is dangerous. It inherits any bias in the training model, and it adds its own approximation error. Honest use pairs every surrogate prediction with a validation estimate of that error. In Kronos design work, surrogates stand in for costly transport and electromagnetic simulations of the Hyperion breeder so that parameter scans finish in interactive time, but every scan result is checked against a full-fidelity run before it informs a decision.
Surrogates do not replace the physics; they compress access to it.

title: Response Surface Methodology
lede: Response surface methodology fits low-order polynomials to sampled data to map how outputs respond to inputs and to locate optima.
body: Response surface methodology (RSM) grew out of industrial experiment design in the mid-twentieth century. It approximates an unknown response y = f(x) with a simple polynomial - usually linear or quadratic - fit by least squares to a set of designed experiments. The fitted surface is then used to understand trends and to move toward an optimum.

A second-order response surface has the form y = b0 + sum(b_i x_i) + sum(b_ii x_i^2) + sum(b_ij x_i x_j). The linear terms capture main effects, the squared terms capture curvature, and the cross terms capture two-factor interactions. For k inputs this model has (k+1)(k+2)/2 coefficients, so the design must supply at least that many distinct runs.
Central composite designs add axial and center points to a factorial base to estimate curvature
Box-Behnken designs avoid extreme corner combinations
Factorial and fractional-factorial designs estimate main effects and interactions economically

Coefficients come from ordinary least squares. The fit is judged by the coefficient of determination, adjusted R-squared, lack-of-fit tests against replicated points, and residual plots. Because the model is deliberately simple, RSM is most reliable over a small, local region of the input space where a quadratic is a fair approximation of the true response.

When the current region is far from an optimum, the gradient of the fitted linear surface points the direction of steepest ascent. Experiments march along that path until improvement stalls, then a new local quadratic is fit to find the peak precisely. This sequential strategy is the classic RSM optimization loop.

A global quadratic cannot represent multi-modal or sharply nonlinear responses. For those, RSM gives way to richer surrogates: polynomial chaos, Gaussian processes, or neural networks. Still, RSM remains the fastest way to screen a handful of design variables and to get an interpretable first map of a response before committing to heavier machinery.

title: Design of Experiments for Surrogates
lede: Design of experiments chooses where to sample an expensive model so a surrogate learns the most from the fewest runs.
body: Every surrogate is only as good as the points it was trained on. Design of experiments (DoE) is the discipline of placing those points deliberately rather than randomly, so that a fixed sampling budget yields the most accurate and least biased surrogate.

Classical designs - full factorial, fractional factorial, central composite, Box-Behnken - were built for polynomial response surfaces and physical experiments with replication and noise. Computer experiments are deterministic: the same input gives the same output every time, so replication adds nothing. For deterministic simulators the goal shifts to space-filling designs that spread points evenly across the whole domain.
Latin hypercube sampling stratifies each input dimension so every level is represented once
Maximin and minimax designs maximize the minimum distance between points to avoid clustering
Low-discrepancy sequences (Sobol, Halton) fill space with near-uniform coverage
Orthogonal-array-based designs control projections onto low-dimensional subspaces

Common optimality criteria include D-optimality (minimize the volume of the coefficient confidence ellipsoid), I-optimality (minimize average prediction variance), and maximin distance. For Gaussian-process surrogates, integrated mean-squared prediction error is a natural target because it ties the design directly to predictive quality.

A one-shot design fixes all sample locations before any run. A sequential or adaptive design runs an initial batch, fits a surrogate, and then chooses the next point where the surrogate is most uncertain or where an optimum is likely. Sequential designs are usually more efficient because they let observed structure guide later sampling.

A rough starting budget for a smooth response is roughly ten samples per input dimension, refined by validation error. High-dimensional problems demand dimension reduction or screening first, because uniform coverage becomes impossible as dimensions grow. In Kronos parameter studies of the Hyperion breeder, an initial Latin hypercube over field, current, and shaping variables seeds the surrogate, and adaptive points are added where predictive variance is largest.

title: Polynomial Chaos Expansion
lede: Polynomial chaos expands a model output as a series of orthogonal polynomials in the random inputs, giving a surrogate and uncertainty statistics at once.
body: Polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) represents an uncertain output Y as a spectral series in the random inputs: Y = sum over alpha of c_alpha * Psi_alpha(xi), where xi are standard random variables, Psi_alpha are multivariate orthogonal polynomials, and c_alpha are deterministic coefficients. The expansion is truncated to a finite set of terms, typically all polynomials up to a chosen total degree.

The Wiener-Askey scheme matches the polynomial basis to the input distribution so the basis stays orthogonal under that distribution. Gaussian inputs pair with Hermite polynomials, uniform inputs with Legendre, beta with Jacobi, gamma with Laguerre. Correct pairing gives fast convergence; a mismatch degrades it.
Intrusive (Galerkin) projection rewrites the governing equations for the coefficients - accurate but requires modifying the solver
Non-intrusive projection estimates coefficients by numerical quadrature over sampled runs - treats the solver as a black box
Regression (least-squares or sparse) fits coefficients to a design of experiments and scales better to many inputs

Because the basis is orthonormal, the mean of Y equals the coefficient c_0 and the variance equals the sum of the squares of all other coefficients. Grouping those squared coefficients by which inputs they involve yields Sobol sensitivity indices directly, with no extra sampling. This is one of PCE's most useful properties.

The number of terms grows combinatorially: for d inputs and total degree p there are (d+p)!/(d! p!) terms. For high-dimensional problems this is prohibitive, which motivates sparse PCE that keeps only significant terms via compressed-sensing or adaptive basis selection.

PCE converges spectrally fast for smooth responses with a moderate number of inputs and gives both a surrogate and closed-form uncertainty statistics. It struggles with discontinuities, sharp bifurcations, and very high input dimension. In Kronos work it is used to propagate uncertainty in a handful of physics parameters through reduced transport models where the response is smooth.

title: Gaussian-Process Surrogates
lede: A Gaussian process treats an unknown function as a distribution over functions, giving interpolated predictions with calibrated error bars.
body: A Gaussian process (GP) is a probability distribution over functions such that any finite set of function values has a joint Gaussian distribution. It is fully specified by a mean function m(x) and a covariance (kernel) function k(x, x'). Training data are treated as observed samples of this random function, and prediction is conditioning on those observations.

Given training inputs X with outputs y, the predictive distribution at a new point x* is Gaussian. The predictive mean is a weighted average of the training outputs, and the predictive variance grows with distance from training points. This variance is the surrogate's own error bar - the single most valuable feature of GP regression for uncertainty quantification and active learning.

With kernel matrix K on training points, cross-covariance vector k* to the test point, and noise variance sigma^2, the predictive mean is k*^T (K + sigma^2 I)^{-1} y and the predictive variance is k(x*,x*) - k*^T (K + sigma^2 I)^{-1} k*. The matrix inverse makes naive GP training scale as the cube of the number of points.
Squared-exponential (RBF) kernels assume very smooth functions
Matern kernels allow tunable roughness and are often more realistic
Length-scale hyperparameters set how fast the function can vary per input
Automatic relevance determination gives each input its own length scale, revealing which inputs matter

Hyperparameters are usually chosen by maximizing the log marginal likelihood, which balances data fit against model complexity automatically. This built-in Occam penalty makes GPs resistant to overfitting on small datasets.

GPs excel with small to moderate datasets, interpolate exactly through noise-free data, and quantify their own uncertainty. Their cubic scaling and difficulty in very high dimensions are the main limits, addressed by sparse and inducing-point approximations. In Kronos design, GP surrogates map costly equilibrium and transport runs of the Hyperion breeder and flag exactly where more full-fidelity runs are needed.

title: Kriging
lede: Kriging is Gaussian-process interpolation born in geostatistics, predicting a spatial field as a best linear unbiased estimate from nearby samples.
body: Kriging is named for mining engineer Danie Krige and formalized by Georges Matheron. It was created to estimate ore grade at unsampled locations from drill-hole data. Mathematically it is identical to Gaussian-process regression, and the two names are used interchangeably depending on the field.

Kriging predicts the value at a new location as a weighted linear combination of observed values, choosing the weights to be unbiased and to minimize prediction variance. The weights depend on the spatial correlation structure, which is captured by the variogram - a plot of how variance between two points grows with their separation.
Simple kriging assumes a known constant mean
Ordinary kriging estimates an unknown constant mean from the data
Universal kriging models a spatially varying trend plus correlated residuals
Co-kriging uses a correlated secondary variable to sharpen predictions of a primary one

The empirical variogram is fit with a model - spherical, exponential, or Gaussian - characterized by a nugget (measurement noise at zero distance), a sill (the plateau variance), and a range (the distance beyond which points are effectively uncorrelated). These parameters play the same role as GP kernel hyperparameters.

In computer experiments, kriging fits a deterministic simulator's response over a design space. The nugget is often set to zero because the simulator is noise-free, making the surrogate interpolate the training runs exactly. The kriging variance then serves as an error estimate that drives adaptive sampling, as in efficient global optimization.

Kriging gives smooth interpolation, honest uncertainty, and interpretable correlation parameters from modest data. Its cubic cost with sample count is the main constraint. Across Kronos design studies, kriging surrogates of field solvers let engineers estimate a quantity anywhere in the design space and know how much to trust each estimate before spending a full simulation.

title: Radial Basis Function Surrogates
lede: Radial basis function interpolants build a surrogate from weighted bumps centered on training points, giving smooth fits with simple linear algebra.
body: A radial basis function (RBF) surrogate represents the response as f_hat(x) = sum of w_i * phi(||x - x_i||), a weighted sum of basis functions that depend only on the distance from each training center x_i. Because each basis is radially symmetric about its center, the method extends cleanly to any number of input dimensions.
Gaussian: phi(r) = exp(-(epsilon r)^2), compact and smooth
Multiquadric: phi(r) = sqrt(1 + (epsilon r)^2), globally supported
Thin-plate spline: phi(r) = r^2 log r, parameter-free and popular for smooth surfaces

Requiring the interpolant to pass through every training point gives a linear system Phi w = y, where Phi is the matrix of basis values between all pairs of centers. Solving this system once yields the weights; evaluation afterward is a fast sum. For conditionally positive-definite bases like multiquadrics, a low-order polynomial term is added with side constraints to guarantee a unique solution.

Gaussian and multiquadric bases carry a shape parameter epsilon that sets how wide each bump is. Small epsilon (flat bumps) gives high accuracy but an ill-conditioned matrix; large epsilon is stable but less accurate. Choosing epsilon by cross-validation is a routine but delicate step; the trade-off is sometimes called the uncertainty principle of RBF interpolation.

RBFs are meshfree, handle scattered data in high dimensions, and are cheap to evaluate once fit. Unlike Gaussian processes they do not natively provide error bars, though a probabilistic reinterpretation recovers them. Dense global bases produce a full linear system that scales poorly to very large datasets unless compactly supported bases are used.

RBF surrogates are a workhorse for surrogate-based optimization and for reconstructing smooth engineering fields from a handful of expensive runs. In Kronos scans they provide fast interpolants where a full probabilistic treatment is unnecessary and only a smooth response map is needed.

title: Reduced-Order Models
lede: Reduced-order models compress a high-dimensional simulation onto a few dominant modes, keeping the physics while cutting the cost by orders of magnitude.
body: A full simulation may carry millions of state variables - the temperature or field at every mesh point. Yet the solution often lives near a low-dimensional manifold: a few patterns explain most of the variation. A reduced-order model (ROM) projects the governing equations onto a small basis of such patterns, turning a huge system into a small one that captures the essential dynamics.

The workhorse approach collects snapshots of the full solution, extracts a low-dimensional basis (commonly by proper orthogonal decomposition), and uses Galerkin or Petrov-Galerkin projection to write reduced governing equations for the coefficients on that basis. The reduced equations retain the original physical structure - conservation laws, nonlinearities - unlike a purely data-fit surrogate.
Intrusive ROMs project the actual equations and need access to the solver's operators
Non-intrusive ROMs learn the reduced dynamics from snapshot data alone, treating the solver as a black box
Operator inference sits between: it fits reduced operators of a known form from data

For nonlinear systems, evaluating the projected nonlinear term still touches the full state, erasing the speedup. Hyper-reduction methods - the discrete empirical interpolation method and its variants - sample the nonlinear term at a few points and reconstruct it, restoring genuine efficiency.

Design and control need the model across a range of parameters, not one operating point. Parametric ROMs interpolate reduced bases or operators across parameter space, or build a global basis spanning several regimes, so one reduced model serves the whole design envelope.

A ROM inherits error from truncating the basis and from hyper-reduction. Rigorous a posteriori error estimators bound the gap to the full model for certain problem classes. In Kronos engineering, ROMs of electromagnetic and thermal-structural solvers give fast, physics-consistent evaluations for the Hyperion breeder, and each ROM is validated against full-order runs before it is used to screen designs.

title: Proper Orthogonal Decomposition
lede: POD finds the optimal linear basis that captures the most energy of a dataset in the fewest modes, the foundation of many reduced-order models.
body: Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) answers a precise question: given a set of snapshots of a field, what orthonormal basis of a given size captures the most variance? The answer is the leading eigenvectors of the snapshot covariance, which are optimal in the least-squares sense. No other linear basis of the same size represents the data with smaller error.

Arrange each snapshot as a column of a matrix A. The singular value decomposition A = U S V^T gives the POD modes as the columns of U, ordered by singular value. Each singular value squared measures the energy captured by its mode. The decay of the singular value spectrum tells you how many modes you need.

A common rule keeps enough modes to capture 99 or 99.9 percent of the cumulative energy - the sum of retained singular values squared over the total. When the spectrum decays fast, a handful of modes suffice; a slowly decaying spectrum warns that the field is not low-rank and a linear ROM will struggle.

POD by itself is a data-compression tool. It becomes a reduced-order model when the governing equations are projected onto the POD basis via Galerkin projection, yielding small ordinary differential equations for the mode coefficients. The quality of the resulting ROM depends entirely on whether the retained modes span the true dynamics, including regimes not present in the snapshots.

POD is optimal for the snapshots it saw. Modes carrying little energy can still be dynamically important - low-energy modes sometimes drive instabilities - so energy truncation can discard critical physics. In Kronos ROM work, POD compresses simulation fields of the Hyperion breeder, and mode selection is checked against the dynamics of interest, not energy alone.

title: Dynamic Mode Decomposition
lede: DMD extracts spatial modes each with a single growth rate and frequency from time-series snapshots, giving a data-driven linear model of dynamics.
body: Dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) analyzes a sequence of time-ordered snapshots and finds spatial patterns that each evolve with a fixed complex frequency - a growth or decay rate plus an oscillation frequency. Where POD gives energetically ranked but dynamically mixed modes, DMD gives modes with clean temporal behavior, making it a data-driven approximation of the system's dynamics.

DMD assumes snapshots are related by an unknown linear map A: x_{k+1} = A x_k. It finds the A that best fits the data in a least-squares sense, then computes A's eigenvalues and eigenvectors. The eigenvectors are the DMD modes; the eigenvalues encode each mode's growth rate and frequency. A is never formed explicitly for large states - it is represented on a POD subspace.
Stack snapshots into matrices X (times 1..n-1) and X' (times 2..n)
Take the SVD of X to get a reduced basis
Project to form a small matrix A-tilde and compute its eigendecomposition
Map eigenvectors back to full space to get DMD modes; eigenvalues give dynamics

DMD is the leading numerical method for approximating the Koopman operator, which represents even nonlinear dynamics as a linear operator acting on observables. This connection explains why DMD can capture some nonlinear behavior and motivates extended DMD, which enriches the observable set with nonlinear functions of the state.

DMD is used to identify coherent structures, estimate stability, forecast short-term evolution, and detect regime changes. Variants handle control inputs (DMD with control), noise (total-least-squares DMD), and sparse or streaming data. Unlike a Galerkin ROM it needs no equations, only measurements.

DMD is fundamentally a linear-in-time model, so strongly nonlinear or chaotic dynamics defeat plain DMD. Its modes depend on snapshot spacing and window length. In Kronos diagnostics research, DMD is a candidate for extracting dominant modes and growth rates from time-resolved simulation data of plasma behavior in design studies of the machines.

title: Deep-Learning Surrogates
lede: Neural networks learn complex, high-dimensional input-output maps from simulation data, serving as fast surrogates where classical methods struggle.
body: Classical surrogates - polynomials, Gaussian processes, RBFs - handle smooth responses in modest dimensions well but strain when inputs number in the hundreds, outputs are whole fields, or the response is sharply nonlinear. Deep neural networks are universal approximators that scale to such regimes, learning the map f: x to y directly from a large set of simulation samples.
Fully connected networks for scalar or low-dimensional outputs
Convolutional networks for outputs on regular grids, such as field snapshots
Graph neural networks for outputs on unstructured meshes
Recurrent and transformer models for time-series and sequence outputs
Autoencoders to compress fields into a latent space before regression

The network minimizes a loss - typically mean-squared error - over the training set by stochastic gradient descent with backpropagation. Because simulation data is expensive, neural surrogates are hungry for samples, so techniques like data augmentation, transfer learning from cheaper models, and physics-based regularization are used to make the most of limited runs.

A plain network gives a point prediction with no error bar. Uncertainty is added by deep ensembles (train several networks and use their spread), Monte Carlo dropout (sample networks at test time), Bayesian neural networks (distributions over weights), or by predicting a mean and variance jointly. Any deployment for decision-making needs one of these to avoid overconfident predictions.

Neural surrogates interpolate well but extrapolate poorly and unpredictably outside their training distribution, often with high confidence. They can also violate physical constraints - conservation, symmetry, monotonicity - unless those are enforced by architecture or loss. This makes validation on held-out and out-of-distribution data essential.

Deep surrogates are attractive for emulating expensive transport, equilibrium, and disruption models across wide operating spaces. In Kronos studies they are trained on full-fidelity simulation data of the machines, always paired with uncertainty estimates and checked against physics-based baselines before informing design choices; nothing they produce substitutes for a hardware result.

title: Neural Operators
lede: Neural operators learn mappings between function spaces, so one trained model solves a family of PDEs at any resolution.
body: A standard neural surrogate learns a map from a fixed input vector to a fixed output vector. A neural operator learns a map between whole functions - for example from an initial condition or coefficient field to the solution of a partial differential equation. Once trained, it approximates the solution operator of the PDE for a range of inputs, not a single instance.

The defining property of a neural operator is that it is discretization-invariant: trained on data at one mesh resolution, it can be queried at a finer or coarser resolution without retraining. This distinguishes it from a convolutional surrogate tied to a fixed grid, and it means the operator represents a continuous mapping rather than a matrix of a fixed size.
Fourier neural operators apply learnable filters in the Fourier domain, capturing global structure efficiently
Graph neural operators pass messages on a graph to handle irregular geometries
DeepONet uses a branch network for the input function and a trunk network for the query location
Wavelet and spectral variants target multiscale or non-periodic problems

The Fourier neural operator transforms the input to the frequency domain, multiplies by learned weights on the low frequency modes, transforms back, and adds a local linear term, repeating over several layers. Truncating to low modes gives efficiency and a smoothing prior well suited to many physical fields.

Neural operators can emulate PDE solvers orders of magnitude faster and generalize across inputs and resolutions. They still require substantial training data, can struggle with sharp fronts and shocks, and extrapolate poorly beyond the training distribution. Uncertainty quantification for operators is an active research area.

For fusion design, neural operators are a candidate for emulating field solvers whose inputs are spatial profiles rather than a few scalars. In Kronos research they are evaluated as fast emulators of electromagnetic and transport fields for the machines, subject to the same validation discipline as any surrogate.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks
lede: PINNs embed the governing equations into a network's loss, so the surrogate respects physics and can train with little or no labeled data.
body: A physics-informed neural network (PINN) represents the solution of a differential equation as a neural network of the input coordinates. Instead of fitting only to data, its loss includes the residual of the governing equation evaluated at sampled collocation points, plus terms for boundary and initial conditions. Automatic differentiation computes the needed derivatives of the network exactly.

The total loss is a weighted sum: a data term matching any available measurements, a PDE-residual term forcing the equation to hold at collocation points, and boundary and initial condition terms. Minimizing it drives the network toward a function that both fits data and satisfies the physics, so labeled solution data can be sparse or absent.
Solving forward problems where the equation is known
Inverse problems - inferring unknown coefficients or sources from sparse measurements
Assimilating noisy data while enforcing conservation laws
Filling gaps where measurements are missing but physics constrains the field

Training PINNs is notoriously delicate. The competing loss terms need careful weighting; stiff, multiscale, or high-frequency problems suffer from spectral bias where the network learns smooth components first and struggles with sharp features. Convergence can be slow, and a converged PINN is not guaranteed to be the correct solution without verification.

Domain decomposition splits hard problems into subdomains; adaptive collocation places more points where the residual is large; variational and energy-based formulations lower the derivative order; and hard-constraint architectures build boundary conditions into the network so they hold exactly rather than approximately.

PINNs blur the line between solver and surrogate: they can act as mesh-free solvers or as data-physics hybrids. In Kronos research they are studied as inverse-problem tools - inferring hidden parameters from limited diagnostics under physical constraints - with results always cross-checked against conventional discretized solvers of the machines' physics.

title: Active Learning for Surrogates
lede: Active learning lets a surrogate choose its own next training point, spending expensive evaluations where they most improve accuracy.
body: When each training sample requires an hours-long simulation, sampling blindly wastes the budget. Active learning closes a loop: fit a surrogate on current data, use it to decide the most informative place to evaluate the expensive model next, run there, add the result, and repeat. The surrogate steers its own data collection.

The choice of next point is governed by an acquisition function that scores candidate locations. For a Gaussian-process surrogate, predictive variance is a natural score - sample where the model is least certain. Other criteria target integrated mean-squared error reduction, expected model change, or query-by-committee disagreement among an ensemble of surrogates.
For a global surrogate: sample to reduce prediction variance everywhere
For optimization: sample where an optimum is likely (expected improvement)
For a failure boundary or contour: sample near the level set of interest
For rare-event probability: sample near the limit-state surface

Active learning needs a surrogate that reports where it is uncertain. This is why Gaussian processes and Bayesian methods dominate the field: their predictive variance is a ready-made acquisition signal. Deterministic surrogates need an ensemble or a bootstrap to estimate uncertainty before they can be used actively.

Modern compute lets several expensive runs proceed at once, so batch active learning selects a diverse set of points that are individually informative and jointly non-redundant. This requires penalizing points that are close together, since two nearby samples teach almost the same lesson.

Active learning routinely reaches a target accuracy with a fraction of the samples that space-filling designs need, especially when the response has localized complex regions. In Kronos parameter studies, surrogates of the Hyperion breeder request full-fidelity runs adaptively - concentrating effort near operating boundaries and steep gradients rather than spreading it uniformly across a mostly smooth space.

title: Adaptive Sampling
lede: Adaptive sampling adds training points sequentially where a surrogate is weakest, balancing exploration of unseen regions against refinement of complex ones.
body: A fixed space-filling design spends its budget before it knows where the response is difficult. Adaptive sampling instead grows the training set in stages: build a surrogate, identify where it needs help, evaluate the expensive model there, and refit. Each stage uses everything learned so far to place the next points.

Two forces compete. Exploration seeks under-sampled regions to guard against surprises far from existing points. Exploitation refines regions where the surrogate already sees strong nonlinearity or high error. A good adaptive criterion blends both, often by combining a distance-based space-filling term with a local error or variance term.
Predictive variance - refine where a Gaussian process is uncertain
Cross-validation error - refine where leave-one-out predictions fail
Gradient or curvature - refine where the response changes fastest
Expected improvement - refine near suspected optima for optimization tasks
Maximin distance - explore the largest empty gaps

Many engineering questions concern a threshold: where does a stress exceed a limit, or a plasma cross a stability boundary. Contour-oriented adaptive sampling concentrates points along the level set of interest, resolving that boundary sharply while ignoring regions far from it, which is far more efficient than uniform refinement.

Adaptive sampling stops when a convergence metric plateaus - cross-validation error, maximum predictive variance, or the change in a quantity of interest between iterations falls below a tolerance - or when the evaluation budget is exhausted. A clear stopping rule prevents both under-training and wasted runs.

Adaptive sampling is the engine behind efficient global optimization and reliability analysis with surrogates. In Kronos design work it places full-fidelity runs of the machines where operating limits and nonlinear response make them most valuable, so a limited simulation budget yields a surrogate that is accurate exactly where decisions are made.

title: Uncertainty Quantification Overview
lede: Uncertainty quantification turns a single model prediction into a distribution, tracing how input, model, and data uncertainties shape the answer.
body: Why a point answer is not enough

A simulation that reports one number hides how much that number could change if inputs, model choices, or data were slightly different. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is the discipline of characterizing, propagating, and reducing uncertainty so predictions come with defensible error bars and so decisions account for what is unknown.
Parametric - uncertain input values such as material properties or reaction rates
Model-form - the equations themselves are approximate
Numerical - discretization, truncation, and solver tolerance error
Data - measurement noise and limited observations
Aleatoric - irreducible variability in the system itself

Forward UQ pushes known input uncertainties through the model to find the output distribution. Inverse UQ uses observed data to infer uncertain inputs or parameters, typically in a Bayesian framework. A full study often does inverse UQ to calibrate a model, then forward UQ to make predictions with the calibrated uncertainties.

Monte Carlo and quasi-Monte Carlo sampling, polynomial chaos expansions, Gaussian-process emulators, and multilevel methods propagate uncertainty. Sensitivity analysis, especially Sobol indices, apportions output variance among inputs. Bayesian inference calibrates parameters and quantifies epistemic uncertainty. Surrogates make all of these affordable for expensive models.

Rigorous UQ can demand thousands to millions of model evaluations - impossible with an hours-long simulation. Surrogates stand in for the expensive model so the sampling completes in reasonable time. The surrogate's own approximation error then becomes another uncertainty source that must be accounted for, not ignored.

Credible UQ states its assumptions, separates what is reducible from what is not, and validates its uncertainty estimates against reality. In Kronos design, UQ propagates uncertainty in physics parameters through models of the machines, distinguishing what more data could tighten from what is inherent, and never presents a simulated prediction as a measured result.

title: Aleatoric versus Epistemic Uncertainty
lede: Aleatoric uncertainty is inherent randomness you cannot reduce; epistemic uncertainty is ignorance you can reduce with more data or better models.
body: Uncertainty splits into two categories that behave differently and demand different responses. Aleatoric uncertainty (from the Latin for dice) is the irreducible variability of a system - genuine randomness that persists no matter how much you learn. Epistemic uncertainty (from the Greek for knowledge) is due to limited information and shrinks as you gather more data or improve the model.
Aleatoric: thermal noise in a sensor, turbulent fluctuations, manufacturing scatter across nominally identical parts
Epistemic: an imprecisely known reaction rate, an untested model assumption, a parameter fit from too few samples

The two call for opposite strategies. You cannot buy down aleatoric uncertainty with more experiments - only by changing the system or accepting the spread. Epistemic uncertainty is a to-do list: more measurements, better physics, or more training samples will reduce it. Confusing the two leads to wasted effort on the irreducible or false confidence about the reducible.

In a probabilistic model, aleatoric uncertainty is often modeled as observation noise - a variance term on the output. Epistemic uncertainty appears as uncertainty in parameters or model structure - a distribution over weights, a Gaussian-process posterior variance, or the spread across an ensemble. A Gaussian process, for instance, separates its predictive variance into a noise floor (aleatoric) and a distance-dependent term that vanishes near data (epistemic).

Total predictive uncertainty is the combination of both. Deep ensembles and Bayesian neural networks that predict both a mean and a variance can decompose their output uncertainty into the two parts, which is valuable for deciding whether more data would help.

For Kronos models, plasma turbulence and shot-to-shot variability are aleatoric, while imperfectly known transport coefficients and model-form choices are epistemic. Separating them clarifies which uncertainties in the machines' predicted performance more experiments can tighten and which reflect the physics itself.

title: Forward Uncertainty Propagation
lede: Forward UQ pushes known input distributions through a model to compute the resulting distribution, moments, and failure probabilities of the output.
body: Given uncertain inputs described by probability distributions, forward uncertainty propagation asks: what is the distribution of the output? The goal may be the mean and variance, the full probability density, a quantile, or the probability that the output exceeds a safety threshold. It is the most common UQ task in engineering design.

Monte Carlo is the baseline: draw input samples from their distributions, evaluate the model for each, and build output statistics from the results. It is simple, dimension-independent in convergence rate, and robust, but its error shrinks only as one over the square root of the sample count, so it needs many runs. Quasi-Monte Carlo and Latin hypercube sampling improve this for smooth problems.
Polynomial chaos expansions give mean, variance, and Sobol indices in closed form for smooth responses
Gaussian-process emulators propagate uncertainty with error bars from few runs
Stochastic collocation evaluates on a sparse grid of quadrature points
The delta method uses a first-order Taylor expansion for small uncertainties

For small input uncertainties, a first-order Taylor expansion propagates variance cheaply: output variance is approximately the sum over inputs of (partial derivative)^2 times input variance. This linearization is fast but fails for nonlinear responses or large uncertainties, where full sampling is required.

When the quantity of interest is a small failure probability, plain Monte Carlo is inefficient because failures are rare. Importance sampling, subset simulation, and first- and second-order reliability methods concentrate effort near the failure boundary to estimate small probabilities with far fewer runs.

Forward UQ turns a Kronos performance prediction into a distribution rather than a single figure. Uncertain physics inputs are propagated through surrogates of the machines to report expected performance with credible intervals, and to estimate the chance of crossing an operating limit - always distinguishing simulated ranges from any future measured result.

title: Inverse Uncertainty Quantification
lede: Inverse UQ infers uncertain model parameters from observed data, returning distributions that reflect what the data can and cannot pin down.
body: Forward UQ assumes input uncertainties are known and computes the output. Inverse UQ runs the other way: given measurements of the output, what were the inputs or parameters, and how uncertain are they? The answer is not a single best-fit value but a distribution that captures every parameter combination consistent with the data.

Bayes' theorem provides the framework: the posterior distribution of parameters is proportional to the likelihood of the data given the parameters times the prior distribution. The prior encodes what was known beforehand, the likelihood measures fit to data, and the posterior is the updated state of knowledge. Inverse UQ is largely the practice of computing and characterizing this posterior.
Markov chain Monte Carlo draws samples from the posterior without needing its normalizing constant
Sequential Monte Carlo and nested sampling handle multimodal or evidence-computing problems
Variational inference approximates the posterior with a tractable family for speed
The ensemble Kalman filter gives a fast Gaussian approximation for high-dimensional problems

Some parameters cannot be determined from the available data - different values fit equally well. Inverse UQ exposes this through wide or correlated posteriors, which is honest and valuable: it tells you the data is silent on that parameter. Ignoring identifiability produces a confident but meaningless point estimate.

Posterior sampling can require millions of model evaluations, one per proposed parameter set. This is infeasible with an expensive simulator, so a surrogate emulates the model inside the inference loop. The surrogate's approximation error must be included in the likelihood, or the posterior will be falsely narrow.

Inverse UQ calibrates uncertain physics parameters in Kronos models against experimental and literature data, returning posterior ranges rather than tuned single values. This keeps epistemic uncertainty visible and prevents overfitting a model of the machines to sparse observations.

title: Bayesian Calibration of Models
lede: Bayesian calibration tunes model parameters to data while accounting for model discrepancy, yielding parameter posteriors and honest predictions.
body: Calibration adjusts a model's uncertain parameters so its predictions match observations. Bayesian calibration does this probabilistically: it returns a posterior distribution over parameters, propagates that uncertainty into predictions, and - crucially - accounts for the fact that no model is perfect.

The influential Kennedy and O'Hagan formulation writes an observation as the model output at the true parameters, plus a model discrepancy term, plus observation noise. The discrepancy term - itself modeled as a Gaussian process - captures the systematic gap between model and reality. Ignoring it causes calibration to compensate by pushing parameters to unphysical values that fit data for the wrong reason.
A prior over the physical parameters, from theory or prior experiments
A likelihood linking model plus discrepancy plus noise to the data
A surrogate emulator of the expensive model for tractable inference
A discrepancy model to absorb structural error

Parameters and the discrepancy term can trade off against each other - a phenomenon called confounding. Strong priors, multiple experimental conditions, and physically constrained discrepancy models help separate genuine parameter values from model error. Without care, a well-fitting calibration can still have meaningless parameter estimates.

The payoff is calibrated prediction: sample parameters from the posterior, run the model (or surrogate), add the discrepancy and noise, and produce a predictive distribution with credible intervals. These intervals reflect parameter uncertainty and known model imperfection together, which is more honest than a single tuned prediction.

Bayesian calibration is the disciplined way to reconcile Kronos physics models with experimental and published data. It yields parameter posteriors and predictive intervals for the machines while keeping model discrepancy explicit, so that agreement with data is not mistaken for a validated point value.

title: Sensitivity Analysis
lede: Sensitivity analysis measures how much each input drives the output, guiding where to focus modeling, measurement, and uncertainty reduction.
body: Given a model with many uncertain inputs, sensitivity analysis asks which inputs matter. It ranks inputs by their influence on the output, revealing what to measure more precisely, what to hold fixed, and where model error will hurt most. It is the natural companion to uncertainty propagation.

Local sensitivity analysis computes partial derivatives of the output with respect to each input at a nominal point - the response to a small nudge. It is cheap but valid only near that point and blind to interactions. Global sensitivity analysis explores the whole input space and captures nonlinearity and interactions, at greater cost.
Variance-based Sobol indices apportion output variance to inputs and their interactions
The Morris elementary-effects method screens many inputs cheaply
Derivative-based global measures average local gradients over the space
Regression-based indices use standardized coefficients on sampled data

A common two-stage strategy uses a cheap screening method - such as Morris - to discard clearly unimportant inputs, then applies an expensive quantitative method like Sobol only to the survivors. This keeps the analysis affordable when inputs number in the dozens or hundreds.

Inputs rarely act alone. Two inputs may each look unimportant individually yet strongly influence the output together. Only methods that account for interactions - Sobol total-effect indices in particular - reveal this. Ranking by main effects alone can badly mislead when interactions are strong.

Global sensitivity analysis needs many model evaluations, so it is usually run on a surrogate. Polynomial chaos even yields Sobol indices analytically from its coefficients. In Kronos studies, sensitivity analysis identifies which physics parameters dominate predicted performance of the machines, directing where tighter data and better models pay off most.

title: Sobol Sensitivity Indices
lede: Sobol indices decompose output variance into contributions from each input and every interaction, giving a rigorous global sensitivity measure.
body: Sobol indices rest on the ANOVA decomposition of a function into a sum of terms: a mean, one term per input, one per pair of inputs, and so on. Because these terms are orthogonal, the total output variance splits cleanly into contributions from each input alone and from each interaction. Sobol indices are those contributions expressed as fractions of the total variance.

The first-order index S_i is the fraction of output variance explained by input i acting alone - the expected variance reduction if i were fixed. The total-effect index S_Ti includes i's main effect plus all its interactions - the variance that would remain if every input except i were fixed. The gap between S_Ti and S_i measures how much i acts through interactions.
S_i near zero and S_Ti near zero: input i is unimportant and can be fixed
S_i near S_Ti: i acts mainly on its own, interactions are weak
S_Ti much larger than S_i: i matters chiefly through interactions
First-order indices summing near one: the model is nearly additive

The classic estimator uses two independent sample matrices and a set of hybrid matrices, costing N times (d+2) model evaluations for d inputs. This is expensive, so Sobol indices are typically computed on a surrogate. Polynomial chaos gives them for free by grouping squared coefficients by the inputs they involve.

Standard Sobol indices assume independent inputs; correlated inputs require generalized or Shapley-based extensions. Variance is only a complete summary when the output distribution is not heavy-tailed or multimodal; otherwise moment-independent measures may be preferable.

Sobol analysis of Kronos models quantifies how much each uncertain physics parameter contributes to the variance in predicted machine performance, and how strongly parameters interact. This focuses measurement and model-improvement effort on the inputs that actually control the outcome.

title: The Morris Screening Method
lede: The Morris method screens many inputs with few runs, flagging which are negligible, which are linear, and which are nonlinear or interacting.
body: When a model has dozens or hundreds of uncertain inputs, a full variance-based analysis is too expensive to start with. The Morris method - also called the elementary effects method - provides a global screening at a fraction of the cost, identifying which inputs are worth deeper study and which can be safely fixed.

An elementary effect for input i is the change in output when i is perturbed by a fixed step, divided by the step, holding other inputs at a sampled point. The method computes several such effects for each input from different starting points scattered across the input space, so the effects are global rather than tied to one location.

Morris uses efficient trajectories through input space: from a random starting point, each input is stepped once in turn. A trajectory of d+1 runs yields one elementary effect per input. Repeating for r trajectories costs r times (d+1) runs - linear in the number of inputs, far cheaper than variance methods.
mu-star: the mean of the absolute elementary effects, measuring overall influence
sigma: the standard deviation of the effects, measuring nonlinearity and interaction

Plotting sigma against mu-star classifies inputs. Low mu-star and low sigma means negligible. High mu-star and low sigma means an important, roughly linear effect. High sigma means the input is nonlinear or interacts with others - its effect depends on where you are in input space. This diagnosis guides the next, more detailed analysis.

Morris is the standard first pass before Sobol analysis. In Kronos model studies with many uncertain parameters, it inexpensively separates the handful of influential physics inputs from the many that barely move the machines' predicted performance, so that costly variance-based analysis is spent only where it matters.

title: Local versus Global Sensitivity
lede: Local sensitivity measures the response to a small nudge at one point; global sensitivity averages influence over the whole uncertain input space.
body: Two scopes of the same question

Both approaches ask how inputs affect an output, but over different scopes. Local sensitivity examines the neighborhood of a single nominal point. Global sensitivity examines the entire range of plausible inputs. The right choice depends on whether the model is near-linear and whether inputs vary a little or a lot.

Local sensitivity is the vector of partial derivatives of the output with respect to each input, evaluated at a reference point. It answers how a small change in each input moves the output there. It is cheap - one gradient, often available by finite differences or automatic differentiation - and it underlies gradient-based optimization and first-order error propagation.
Valid only near the reference point; a different point can give different rankings
Misses nonlinearity - a derivative is a straight-line approximation
Depends on input scaling unless the derivatives are normalized

Global methods - Sobol indices, Morris effects, regression measures - explore the full input distribution. They capture nonlinear response, interactions, and the effect of large input variation. The price is many model evaluations, which is why they are typically run on surrogates. Their rankings are robust across the input space rather than tied to one location.

Use local analysis when uncertainties are small, the model is smooth, and a reference operating point is well defined - for instance, propagating tight tolerances. Use global analysis when uncertainties are large, the model is nonlinear, or interactions are suspected - the usual situation in early design when the operating point itself is uncertain.

Early Kronos design studies favor global sensitivity because operating parameters span wide ranges and the physics is nonlinear. As a design point for the machines settles, local sensitivity becomes useful for propagating manufacturing and control tolerances around that fixed point.

title: Monte Carlo for Uncertainty Quantification
lede: Monte Carlo estimates output statistics by random sampling of inputs, a robust dimension-independent workhorse of uncertainty propagation.
body: Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation is disarmingly simple: draw many samples of the uncertain inputs from their distributions, run the model on each, and estimate output statistics - mean, variance, quantiles, exceedance probabilities - from the resulting ensemble. Its simplicity, generality, and robustness make it the default against which all other UQ methods are compared.

The Monte Carlo error of a mean estimate shrinks as the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample count N. This rate is independent of the number of input dimensions - a decisive advantage over grid methods that suffer the curse of dimensionality. The cost is slow convergence: cutting the error in half requires four times as many samples.
Unbiased estimates of means and probabilities
Confidence intervals from the sample standard error
Full empirical output distributions, not just moments
No smoothness assumption - works for discontinuous or noisy responses

Because plain Monte Carlo is sample-hungry, variance-reduction techniques squeeze more accuracy from each run: stratified and Latin hypercube sampling spread points more evenly, importance sampling focuses on important regions, control variates exploit a correlated cheap model, and antithetic variates use negatively correlated pairs. Each reduces estimator variance without bias.

Multilevel Monte Carlo runs most samples on cheap low-fidelity models and few on expensive high-fidelity ones, combining them to get high-fidelity accuracy at greatly reduced cost. Multifidelity Monte Carlo generalizes this to arbitrary correlated models, including surrogates. These methods make Monte Carlo affordable for expensive simulators.

Monte Carlo is the reliable backbone of Kronos uncertainty studies. For expensive models of the machines it is run on surrogates or in multifidelity form, and it serves as the trusted reference to check that faster spectral methods have not introduced bias into the reported uncertainty ranges.

title: Quasi-Monte Carlo Methods
lede: Quasi-Monte Carlo replaces random samples with low-discrepancy sequences that fill space more evenly, converging faster than plain Monte Carlo.
body: Random Monte Carlo samples cluster and leave gaps by chance, which slows convergence. Quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) replaces random draws with deterministic low-discrepancy sequences engineered to cover the unit hypercube as uniformly as possible. For smooth integrands this even coverage yields substantially faster convergence.

Discrepancy measures how far a point set departs from perfect uniformity - the largest gap between the fraction of points in any sub-box and that box's volume. Low-discrepancy sequences minimize this. The Koksma-Hlawka inequality bounds integration error by the product of the integrand's variation and the point set's discrepancy, motivating the whole approach.
Sobol sequences - widely used, with good high-dimensional projections
Halton sequences - simple, built from radical inverses in different prime bases
Faure sequences - based on prime-base permutations
Lattice rules - shifted regular lattices tuned for periodic integrands

For sufficiently smooth functions, QMC error decreases roughly as (log N)^d over N - close to order one over N, versus one over the square root of N for random Monte Carlo. In practice this can mean an order of magnitude fewer samples for the same accuracy, though the benefit erodes as dimension d grows and for non-smooth integrands.

Plain QMC gives no built-in error estimate because it is deterministic. Randomized QMC - scrambling or random shifting of the sequence - restores an unbiased estimator and lets you estimate error from a few independent randomizations, combining QMC accuracy with Monte Carlo error bars.

QMC shines for smooth, moderate-dimensional integrals such as propagating a handful of uncertain parameters through a Kronos surrogate. For high effective dimension or discontinuous responses its advantage fades and randomized or plain Monte Carlo may be safer. Choosing the sequence and checking effective dimension are part of using it well.

title: Latin Hypercube Sampling
lede: Latin hypercube sampling stratifies every input dimension so a modest sample covers the space evenly, improving on plain random sampling.
body: Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) divides each input's range into N equal-probability intervals and draws exactly one sample from each interval, then pairs the per-dimension draws at random. The result is that every input is evenly represented across its whole range - no interval is over- or under-sampled - which random sampling cannot guarantee for small N.

The name comes from the Latin square: in a grid, exactly one point per row and per column. LHS generalizes this to many dimensions, so each one-dimensional projection of the sample is perfectly stratified. This gives excellent marginal coverage from few points, a major gain for expensive models.
Split each of the d inputs into N equal-probability bins
Draw one value from each bin per input, giving N values per dimension
Randomly permute the values in each dimension
Combine column by column to form N sample points

Random pairing can still leave spurious correlations between inputs or leave gaps in the joint space. Optimized LHS variants fix this: maximin LHS maximizes the minimum distance between points, and orthogonal-array-based LHS controls low-dimensional projections. These refinements matter most when fitting surrogates that depend on joint structure.

LHS reduces estimator variance for functions dominated by main effects and is a standard default for both UQ sampling and surrogate training designs. Its guarantee is per-dimension, not per joint region, so in high dimensions it does not ensure uniform coverage of the full space the way low-discrepancy sequences aim to. It is also naturally a one-shot design, though extensible variants exist.

LHS is the common starting design for Kronos surrogate builds and Monte Carlo studies: a Latin hypercube over the uncertain physics inputs seeds the training set for models of the machines, after which adaptive sampling adds points where the surrogate is weakest.

title: Importance Sampling
lede: Importance sampling draws from a biased distribution that favors the region of interest, then reweights, to estimate rare events efficiently.
body: Estimating a small probability - say the chance an output exceeds a safety limit - is hard with plain Monte Carlo, because almost no random samples land in the failure region. To see one failure in a probability of one in a million, you need on the order of a million samples. Importance sampling overcomes this by sampling smarter.

Instead of sampling from the true input distribution p, importance sampling draws from a chosen proposal distribution q that puts more mass where the quantity of interest is significant. Each sample is reweighted by the likelihood ratio p(x)/q(x) to remove the bias introduced by using q. The estimator remains unbiased if q covers the support of the integrand.
Shift or scale the input distribution toward the failure region
Center the proposal near the most probable failure point
Use a mixture to cover multiple important regions
Adapt the proposal iteratively as failures are discovered

A well-chosen proposal can cut the required sample count by orders of magnitude. A poor one is worse than plain Monte Carlo: if q misses regions where p is large, a few samples get enormous weights and the estimator's variance explodes. The effective sample size, computed from the weights, diagnoses this degeneracy.

The cross-entropy method automatically tunes the proposal by iteratively fitting it to the samples that came closest to the target region, converging on a near-optimal proposal. Adaptive importance sampling and population Monte Carlo refine the proposal on the fly, reducing the reliance on a good initial guess.

Importance sampling is a core tool for estimating small probabilities of crossing operating or safety limits. In Kronos reliability analysis it concentrates surrogate evaluations near the boundary where a machine parameter would exceed a design limit, estimating small exceedance probabilities that plain Monte Carlo could not resolve within a feasible budget.

title: Error Bars on Predictions
lede: A prediction without an error bar hides how much to trust it; sound surrogates report calibrated uncertainty alongside every value.
body: A single predicted number invites false confidence. An error bar - a standard deviation, a credible interval, or a full predictive distribution - states how much the prediction could plausibly be off. For any decision, the width of the error bar can matter more than the central value, because it governs risk.
Input uncertainty propagated through the model
Surrogate approximation error from limited or poorly placed training data
Observation noise in the data the surrogate learned from
Model-form error - the equations are imperfect

Gaussian processes are the archetype: their predictive variance grows with distance from training points, giving a built-in error bar that is small near data and large in extrapolation. Bayesian methods generally produce full predictive distributions. This self-awareness is what makes such surrogates suitable for active learning and risk-aware design.
Adding error bars to deterministic surrogates

Neural networks and RBF interpolants give point predictions by default. Uncertainty is added by ensembling (train several models and use their spread), bootstrap resampling, Monte Carlo dropout, jackknife or conformal methods, or by training the model to output a variance as well as a mean. Without one of these, such a surrogate is silent about its own reliability.

An error bar is only useful if it is honest: a stated ninety percent interval should contain the truth about ninety percent of the time. Overconfident intervals - too narrow - are dangerous because they hide risk. Calibration is checked on held-out data and corrected if the reported uncertainty does not match observed error frequencies.

Every surrogate-based prediction for the machines carries an uncertainty estimate, and those estimates are validated for calibration. A simulated performance figure is always reported as a range with stated conditions, never as a bare number, and never presented as a measured hardware result before it exists.

title: Prediction versus Confidence Intervals
lede: A confidence interval bounds an estimated parameter; a prediction interval bounds a future observation and is always wider.
body: Confidence intervals and prediction intervals answer different questions and have different widths. Mixing them up leads to error bars that are too narrow for their stated purpose. The difference is whether you are bounding an underlying quantity or an individual future outcome.

A confidence interval bounds a fixed but unknown parameter - a mean, a regression coefficient, a model prediction of the average response. A ninety-five percent confidence interval means that if the experiment were repeated many times, ninety-five percent of the intervals so constructed would contain the true parameter. It captures uncertainty in the estimate, which shrinks as data accumulates.

A prediction interval bounds a single new observation, not a parameter. It must account for both the uncertainty in the estimated model and the inherent random scatter of an individual outcome around the mean. Because it adds this irreducible noise, a prediction interval is always wider than the corresponding confidence interval - and it does not shrink to zero even with infinite data.
Confidence interval width shrinks toward zero as sample size grows
Prediction interval width approaches the noise standard deviation, never zero
Prediction interval variance is roughly confidence variance plus observation variance

The distinction maps onto epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty. A confidence interval reflects epistemic uncertainty about the model, which more data reduces. A prediction interval adds aleatoric noise, which more data does not reduce. A Gaussian process makes this explicit: its posterior mean has a confidence band, and adding the noise variance gives the prediction band.

Report a prediction interval when the audience cares about an individual future outcome - the value a real machine parameter will take on a given shot. Report a confidence interval when the question is about the average or the model's estimate. In Kronos results, the choice is stated explicitly so the error bar matches the claim being made.

title: Validating a Surrogate Model
lede: A surrogate is only trustworthy after validation against data it never saw, on metrics that expose both accuracy and honest uncertainty.
body: A surrogate can match its training data perfectly and still fail everywhere else - the classic overfitting trap. Validation asks the only question that matters: how well does the surrogate predict outputs it was not trained on? This requires data held back from training, or fresh runs of the expensive model at new points.

The simplest check reserves a test set never used in fitting and reports error on it. When data is scarce - the usual case with expensive models - k-fold cross-validation reuses the data by rotating which fold is held out, and leave-one-out cross-validation takes this to the limit. For Gaussian processes, leave-one-out error has an efficient closed form.
Root-mean-square error - overall magnitude of prediction error
Mean absolute error - robust to outliers
Coefficient of determination (R-squared) - fraction of variance explained
Maximum error - the worst-case point, critical for safety limits

For a probabilistic surrogate, accuracy of the mean is not enough - the error bars must be honest too. Coverage tests check that stated intervals contain the truth at the claimed rate. Proper scoring rules such as the continuous ranked probability score and the negative log predictive density reward predictions that are both accurate and well-calibrated.

Average error can hide local failure. Validation should probe the regions that matter - near operating limits, in nonlinear zones, and at the edges of the training domain where extrapolation risk is highest. Out-of-distribution tests reveal how badly the surrogate degrades outside its training envelope.

No Kronos surrogate informs a design decision until it is validated against held-out full-fidelity runs of the machines, on both accuracy and calibration, with attention to behavior near operating boundaries. A surrogate that fails validation is refit with more data or replaced; it is never used on faith.

title: Cross-Validation for Surrogates
lede: Cross-validation reuses scarce data by rotating holdout folds, estimating a surrogate's out-of-sample error without new expensive runs.
body: Making the most of few samples

Surrogates for expensive models are trained on small datasets, so setting aside a large test set is wasteful. Cross-validation solves this by systematically rotating which data serves as the test set, so every point is used for both training and testing across different splits. The averaged error estimates out-of-sample accuracy without spending new evaluations.

The data is split into k equal folds. The surrogate is trained on k-1 folds and tested on the held-out fold, repeated so each fold is held out once. The k test errors are averaged. Common choices are five or ten folds, balancing bias (few folds train on too little data) against variance and cost (many folds are expensive).

Leave-one-out cross-validation takes k equal to the number of samples: each point is predicted from all the others. It uses the most training data per fit and is nearly unbiased, but naively it requires N refits. For linear-in-parameters models and Gaussian processes, an algebraic shortcut computes all leave-one-out errors from a single fit, making it cheap.
Estimating a surrogate's predictive error before deployment
Selecting hyperparameters such as kernel length scales or RBF shape
Comparing candidate surrogate types on the same data
Driving adaptive sampling toward high-error regions

Cross-validation assumes samples are independent; correlated or clustered data - such as points along a design trajectory - inflates optimism unless folds respect the structure. It also tends to be pessimistic for the final model, which trains on all data. And repeatedly tuning to cross-validation error can leak information, so a final untouched test set is still valuable when affordable.

Cross-validation is the routine health check on Kronos surrogates: leave-one-out error guides kernel and hyperparameter choices for models of the machines and flags where the surrogate is unreliable, so adaptive sampling can reinforce those regions.

title: Calibration of Probabilistic Predictions
lede: A well-calibrated model's stated probabilities match observed frequencies, so a ninety percent interval really contains the truth ninety percent of the time.
body: The promise behind an error bar

When a model states a ninety percent prediction interval, it makes a testable promise: over many such predictions, the truth should fall inside about ninety percent of the time. Calibration is whether that promise is kept. A model can be accurate on average yet badly calibrated - confidently wrong - which is often more dangerous than plain inaccuracy.

An overconfident model states intervals that are too narrow, so the truth falls outside more often than claimed. An underconfident model states intervals that are too wide, wasting information. Deep neural networks are notoriously overconfident by default; many surrogates need explicit recalibration before their uncertainty can be trusted.
Reliability diagrams plot predicted probability against observed frequency; the diagonal is perfect
Coverage tests count how often true values fall in stated intervals across a test set
The probability integral transform should be uniform for a calibrated model
Sharpness measures how narrow intervals are, subject to staying calibrated

Proper scoring rules grade probabilistic predictions so that honesty is optimal - the best score is earned by reporting your true belief. The continuous ranked probability score, the negative log predictive density, and the Brier score for classification reward predictions that are both sharp and calibrated, penalizing overconfidence and vagueness alike.

When a model is miscalibrated, post-hoc methods fix the reported probabilities without retraining the mean: temperature scaling adjusts the sharpness of classifier outputs, isotonic and Platt scaling remap predicted probabilities, and conformal prediction wraps any model to produce intervals with guaranteed finite-sample coverage under mild assumptions.

Uncalibrated uncertainty makes risk-based decisions unreliable. In Kronos UQ, the error bars on surrogate predictions for the machines are checked for calibration on held-out data and recalibrated when needed, so that a stated interval means what it says when it informs a design margin.

title: Choosing a Surrogate Model
lede: The right surrogate depends on dimensionality, data budget, smoothness, output type, and whether you need calibrated uncertainty.
body: Every surrogate family embodies assumptions. Choosing well means matching those assumptions to the problem: how many inputs, how many samples you can afford, how smooth and nonlinear the response is, whether outputs are scalars or fields, and whether the task needs honest uncertainty. The wrong match wastes the evaluation budget or produces overconfident predictions.
Input dimension - low favors GPs and polynomial chaos; high favors neural networks with dimension reduction
Sample budget - small favors GPs and RBFs; large enables deep surrogates
Smoothness - smooth favors polynomial chaos and squared-exponential kernels; rough favors Matern or trees
Output type - scalars favor classical surrogates; fields favor POD-based ROMs or neural operators
Uncertainty need - if error bars are required, favor GPs or Bayesian methods

Gaussian processes are the default for small, low-dimensional, smooth problems needing uncertainty. Polynomial chaos suits smooth responses with a handful of inputs where analytic statistics help. Reduced-order models fit field outputs governed by known equations. Neural surrogates earn their keep in high dimensions with abundant data, at the cost of extra machinery for uncertainty.

Rather than choosing on intuition alone, fit several candidates and compare them by cross-validation error and calibration on the same data. This empirical bake-off is often more reliable than theory, especially when the response has unexpected structure. Ensembling several surrogates can beat any single one.

More flexible surrogates fit complex responses but need more data and risk overfitting. Simpler surrogates generalize from little data but may miss structure. The bias-variance trade-off governs this balance; validation, not ambition, should set the model's complexity.

Kronos surrogate work starts simple - a Gaussian process or polynomial chaos on a Latin hypercube design of the machines - and escalates to reduced-order or neural surrogates only when dimensionality or field outputs demand it, with the final choice justified by validation and calibration, not preference.

title: The Curse of Dimensionality
lede: As input dimensions grow, volume explodes and samples spread thin, defeating grid methods and straining every surrogate and UQ technique.
body: The phrase, coined by Richard Bellman, names a family of problems that arise when the number of dimensions grows. The core cause is that the volume of a space grows exponentially with dimension. Ten points cover a line reasonably; the same density on a ten-dimensional cube needs ten billion points. Any method that tries to fill space uniformly becomes hopeless.
Nearest neighbors stop being near - distances to closest and farthest points converge
Random samples all sit near the surface of a high-dimensional ball, not the center
Most of a hypercube's volume lies in its corners
Intuition built in two or three dimensions actively misleads

Grid-based quadrature and full-tensor designs are impossible past a handful of dimensions. Distance-based methods like RBF and Gaussian processes weaken as neighbors lose meaning. The number of polynomial chaos terms explodes combinatorially. The data needed to constrain any flexible model grows exponentially, so accuracy stalls.

Monte Carlo is the great exception: its convergence rate does not depend on dimension, which is why it dominates high-dimensional integration. Sparse grids, low-rank tensor formats, and additive or low-effective-dimension assumptions also help by exploiting structure the full space does not have.

The saving grace is that most real problems have low effective dimension: only a few inputs, or a few combinations of inputs, actually drive the output. Sensitivity analysis, active subspaces, and dimension reduction find this hidden low-dimensional structure and let surrogates work in it rather than in the full space.

Kronos design spaces can nominally involve many parameters, but sensitivity analysis of the machines typically shows a small set of dominant inputs. Surrogates are built in that reduced effective space, and Monte Carlo handles the residual high-dimensional propagation, sidestepping the curse rather than fighting it head-on.

title: Dimensionality Reduction for Surrogates
lede: Reducing inputs or outputs to their essential few directions makes high-dimensional surrogate modeling tractable and more accurate.
body: High-dimensional inputs or outputs make surrogates expensive and inaccurate. Dimensionality reduction finds a smaller set of coordinates that retains the information that matters, then builds the surrogate in that compact space. Done well, it turns an intractable problem into a routine one and often improves accuracy by removing directions that only add noise.

When the output is a whole field - a temperature map, a stress distribution - proper orthogonal decomposition or an autoencoder compresses it to a few coefficients. The surrogate then predicts those coefficients from the inputs, and the full field is reconstructed on demand. This is the standard route to surrogates and reduced-order models for field-valued outputs.
Sensitivity analysis discards inputs that barely affect the output
Active subspaces find the input directions along which the output changes most
Sliced inverse regression finds directions relevant to the response
Principal component analysis compresses correlated inputs

The active subspace method uses the average outer product of the output gradient to identify a few linear combinations of inputs that capture nearly all of the output's variation. The surrogate is built as a function of these combinations. When an active subspace of low dimension exists, high-dimensional problems collapse to one or two effective variables.

Linear methods - PCA, POD, active subspaces - are interpretable and robust and suffice when the data lies near a linear subspace. When it lies on a curved manifold, nonlinear methods - kernel PCA, autoencoders, manifold learning - capture more with fewer dimensions, at the cost of interpretability and more data.

For Kronos models, field outputs of the machines are compressed by POD before a surrogate predicts the mode coefficients, and input screening plus active-subspace analysis reduce many physics parameters to the few effective directions that drive performance, keeping surrogate construction tractable and validated.

title: Multi-Fidelity Surrogates
lede: Multi-fidelity methods combine many cheap approximate runs with few expensive accurate ones to build a surrogate at high-fidelity accuracy for less effort.
body: Most simulations exist at several fidelity levels: a coarse mesh runs in seconds, a fine mesh in hours; a simplified physics model is fast, a full model slow. Low-fidelity models are cheap but biased; high-fidelity models are accurate but costly. Multi-fidelity surrogates fuse them, using the plentiful cheap runs to learn the shape of the response and the few expensive runs to correct the bias.

The methods work when the low-fidelity model is correlated with the high-fidelity one - when it captures trends even if it gets absolute values wrong. The stronger and simpler that relationship, the more the cheap model can substitute for the expensive one. A low-fidelity model that is merely cheap and unrelated adds nothing.
Additive correction: high fidelity equals low fidelity plus a learned discrepancy
Multiplicative correction: high fidelity equals a learned factor times low fidelity
Co-kriging models the two fidelities jointly with correlated Gaussian processes

A widely used scheme models the high-fidelity output as a scaling of the low-fidelity output plus an independent Gaussian-process discrepancy.
